opus-5.5.text:
I think my view has become more pragmatic over time.

Early on, I was quite attracted to the idea of a fully unified, discrete architecture: tokenize everything, whether text, images, audio, or video, into one shared vocabulary and train a single autoregressive model on all of it. It's conceptually very clean. You get one objective, one model, one scaling story, and in principle understanding and generation become the same problem. That elegance was very appealing, especially coming from a language-model background where next-token prediction has worked so remarkably well.

But when you actually try to push it, you run into real friction. The biggest issue is the tokenizer. Discretizing continuous signals like images loses information, and there's a tension between what's good for understanding and what's good for generation. For understanding, you want semantic, abstract representations. For generation, you need fine-grained, pixel-level detail. A single discrete codebook struggles to serve both well. Then there's efficiency: images and video become very long token sequences, and the compute cost goes up quickly.

So now I see "unified" less as a rigid architectural requirement and more as a goal at the level of capability and training. What matters is that the model shares knowledge across modalities and can reason across them, not necessarily that every modality goes through the same discrete bottleneck. Hybrid approaches, like continuous representations for some parts or decoupled encoders for understanding and generation sitting on a shared backbone, may be more practical for now.

That said, I don't think the question is closed. If someone builds a tokenizer that is both semantically rich and high-fidelity, the fully discrete approach could become very attractive again, because the simplicity and scalability benefits are real. So my position is: stay open, follow the empirical results, and don't get too attached to architectural purity. In this field, the thing that scales and actually works usually wins, even if it's less beautiful on paper.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it has shifted quite a bit. When we started, I was very attached to the idea of a single discrete token space for everything: text, images, audio, all flowing through one autoregressive transformer. The elegance was the appeal. If language models scale so well on discrete tokens, why shouldn't vision and speech ride the same train? You tokenize an image with a VQ-style codec, you get a sequence, and the model treats it just like words. One architecture, one training objective, one scaling law.

What changed my mind was spending time with the actual failure modes. Discretizing images throws away a lot. The codebook becomes a bottleneck, and you end up spending enormous model capacity learning to reconstruct texture and fine detail that a continuous representation gives you almost for free. We saw it clearly in understanding tasks: a model fed continuous visual features from a good encoder would read a chart or recognize a small object, and the fully discrete version would stumble on the same input. And on the generation side, the diffusion community kept pulling ahead in quality while we were trying to make token prediction catch up. At some point you have to ask whether you are defending a principle or solving a problem.

So the way I think about it now is to separate two questions I used to conflate. One is unification of the model, meaning a single set of weights that reasons across modalities. The other is unification of the representation, meaning forcing everything into the same discrete form. I still believe strongly in the first. I am much less dogmatic about the second. Text wants to be discrete because language is discrete. Images and audio are fundamentally continuous signals, and pretending otherwise has a cost. A hybrid, where the transformer backbone is shared but the input and output heads are native to each modality, continuous where it makes sense and discrete where it makes sense, now seems more honest to me than the pure version.

I would add that this is not a final answer either. Tokenizers are getting much better, semantic tokenizers in particular, and the gap is narrowing. It is possible that in a few years the discrete approach wins after all, simply because it composes so cleanly with everything else in the LLM stack: the inference infrastructure, the reinforcement learning, the long-context work. So I hold it loosely. The lesson for me was less about discrete versus continuous and more about not letting architectural aesthetics run ahead of the evidence.

astra-6.text:
I’m less convinced that unification has to mean making every modality discrete. A unified architecture is appealing because it lets us share learning across text, images, and audio. But a shared architecture and a shared representation are two different things.

Discretization gives you a convenient interface, but it can also lose information or make the sequence very long. So the question is whether it actually helps the model learn, rather than simply making the design look elegant.

I still think unification is a valuable direction. I’m just more open to a model with a shared core and different representations or objectives for different modalities. For me, the goal is stronger understanding and generation across modalities; a fully discrete architecture is one possible way to get there, rather than the goal itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I’ve become less attached to the idea that unification requires everything to be discrete. There are really two questions: whether different modalities can share an architecture, and whether they should share the same kind of representation. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

Discrete tokens make a unified system very appealing, especially if you want to use the next-token prediction framework. But the representation also has to preserve what matters in each modality. For images or audio, forcing everything through a discrete interface may introduce tradeoffs that the simplicity of the architecture doesn’t justify.

So I would treat a fully discrete architecture as a hypothesis to test, rather than the destination we have to reach. The goal is a model that can understand, generate, and reason across modalities effectively. Whether the best way to achieve that is entirely discrete or a combination of discrete and continuous representations should follow from the results.
